The average person in the US has roughly twice the daily food supply of the average person in Central Africa.

4 maps that explain how the world eats — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ Map one: daily calorie supply per person. The darkest countries are above 3,500 kcal. The pale band across Central and East Africa sits nearer 1,800–2,200. Note the wording — this is food available, not food eaten. Waste isn't subtracted.

2/ Map two: meat supply per person per year. The US, Spain and Portugal run above 100kg. India sits at the far other end, in single digits — by a wide margin the largest low-meat population on Earth, for religious and economic reasons at once.

3/ Map three: undernourishment. Around 9% of humanity, on the order of 700–750 million people, don't get enough energy for an active, healthy life. The deepest reds are Somalia, North Korea, Haiti and Madagascar.
4/ Map four is the same problem from the other side: adult obesity. Above 40% in the US, high across the Gulf, Egypt and the Pacific islands. Under 10% across Japan, Vietnam and much of the Sahel.

5/ Overlay maps three and four and the striking result is how many countries now sit high on both — undernutrition and obesity inside the same population, often the same city. Cheap calories are not the same thing as good ones.

6/ In the early 1960s the world averaged roughly 2,200 kcal per person per day. Today it's nearer 3,000. Humanity solved the calorie problem considerably faster than it solved the distribution problem.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
